paper.title: Generating in the Limit with Infinitely Many Hallucinations
paper.summary: Introduces precision, coverage recall, tail precision, and fractional novelty for generation in the limit, and studies the recall gains available when infinitely many hallucinations are allowed at a vanishing cumulative rate.

formalization_scope.summary: Main result proofs include the 3.5–3.6 half-recall bounds, the 4.6 batched upper bound, Algorithm 7 in 4.9, and E.1/I.3 sharpness. The printed recall clauses of Algorithms 2 and 6 and the unrestricted raw reading of 3.3 have counterexamples.
specializations: The Kleene closure of the source alphabet is represented by natural numbers.

The source algorithms retain histories, counters, chains, intersections, and pods despite a displayed generator type containing only the current adversarial and previous generated sets. Lean exposes the necessary finite adversarial history explicitly.

Theorem 4.3 uses a quadratic adversary-cardinality exploration clock rather than the appendix's output-cardinality pseudocode; it proves the same existential semantic conclusion and preserves every adversarial batch bound.
The independent single-step lower bound uses P15/P39 with target orders compatible with one ambient order.
gaps: The Algorithm 2 and Algorithm 6 recall lower bounds printed in v1 fail on a full single-step input. Whether a different algorithm attains the general k-batched lower guarantee remains separate.
Definition 3.2 raw batches and cumulative increments agree for fresh outputs; their unqualified equivalence in 3.3 fails.
The historical Level 1 statement review applies to its checkpoint. New constructions and counterexamples have kernel checks.

source_assessment.notes: The unbounded constructions are standard. The bounded Theorem 2.1 appendix proof needs an explicit finite-guess case and a cardinality correction when the target-minus-guess enumeration is finite.

formalization.notes: Lean packages both quantified suprema. The bounded precision proof makes the source's standing infinite-guess assumption explicit, separates the finite valid-part case, and uses a capacity-preserving sparse completion in the infinite case.

claims.title: Without novelty: copying guarantee and c-step tightness
claims.statement_summary: Without novelty, copying preserves the adversary's batch bound and recall while attaining lower precision and lower tail precision one. The source also claims that the recall guarantee is tight for c-step generators required to have perfect tail precision for every possible target.

source_assessment.notes: The constructive copying guarantee uses an infinite valid adversarial limit. The separate tightness clause uses a constant output-batch bound c and family-wide perfect tail precision; it does not assert tightness for arbitrary unbounded batch schedules.

formalization.notes: Copying achieves the input recall and the two-target upper bound proves worst-case tightness.

components.summary: The copying generator preserves every adversarial batch bound and recall and attains precision and tail precision one for an infinite valid adversarial limit.

The source indistinguishable-target construction shows that a c-step generator with perfect tail precision for every possible target cannot guarantee recall above the adversary recall bound. This clause uses constant c, separately from the constructive guarantee for arbitrary f.

lean_links.notes: Formalizes the constructive copying component on the normalized universe with an explicit target order. It does not formalize the separate c-step tightness clause of Theorem E.1.

Copying preserves arbitrary input batch bounds. For each recall level in [0,1], one single-step input witnesses the upper bound for all generators with constant batch bounds and perfect tail precision on its limit.
